title: Area VI review: Instrument Approach Procedures
intro: These questions mix all five Tasks of Area VI: non-precision, precision, missed and circling approaches, and the landing. Many of them join two Tasks in one real approach, just like the checkride.

questions.q: You fly the Tallulah LOC RWY 36 shown. Your approach speed is 90 knots true and you have a 10-knot headwind on final. How long after the FAF do you reach the MAP?
questions.why: When the MAP is found by time, figure your groundspeed from approach speed and the wind, and start the clock at the FAF [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. Groundspeed is 90 - 10 = 80 knots. The chart gives 6 NM from the FAF to the MAP [[29:227|IPH Figure 4-58]]: 6 ÷ 80 = 0.075 hr = 4.5 minutes, or 4:30. 4:00 is the table time for 90 knots, which ignores the headwind.

questions.q: You break out above the circling MDA and turn base for the landing runway. The PAPI already shows two white and two red. When should you start down using the PAPI?
options: Now, since two white and two red is on the path
Now, since the PAPI protects you within 10° of centerline
Once you are lined up with the runway on final
Only after you pass the missed approach point
questions.why: Descent using the PAPI should not begin until you are visually aligned with the runway. Its obstacle clearance covers only about 10 degrees either side of the extended centerline, out to 3.4 NM [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]]. When circling, stay no lower than the circling minimums until you are in position for the final descent [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

questions.q: You go missed in a nonradar area. The missed is a climb to 5,000 and hold at the VOR. Climbing through 3,200, Center clears you direct to your alternate at 5,000. What should you do?
options: Keep climbing on the missed until you reach a safe altitude
Turn toward the alternate now and keep climbing
Level at 3,200 and turn, since you are cleared
Turn now; the missed protects you in any direction
questions.why: You must climb to a safe altitude before you leave the published missed approach, especially in a nonradar area. Leaving it before you reach the published altitude may not give enough terrain clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21g]].

questions.q: Your airplane has no published VREF. Its VSO at maximum landing weight is 70 knots. You normally fly approaches at 85 knots. Which category minimums may you use for a circle to land?
options: Category A, because you fly the approach below 91 knots
Category B, because 1.3 VSO is 91 knots
Category A, since VSO is well below 91 knots
Category C, because circling needs one category higher
questions.why: With no VREF, the category comes from 1.3 VSO at maximum landing weight: 1.3 × 70 = 91 knots, and Category B starts at 91 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. The certified category is permanent, and you can never use the minimums of a slower category, even if you fly slower [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

questions.q: You plan the Cheyenne ILS RWY 27 shown. Your airplane has no flight director, no autopilot and no HUD. The ILS line shows RVR 1800 with an asterisk. What visibility minimum applies to you?
options: RVR 1800, since it is printed on the ILS line
RVR 5000, from the inoperative MALSR note
None; the ILS is not authorized without an autopilot
A higher visibility, because RVR 1800 needs an FD, AP or HUD
questions.why: The chart note says RVR 1800 is authorized only with the use of a flight director, autopilot or HUD to the DA [[29:156|IPH Figure 4-8]]. That matches the AIM: a Category I ILS is RVR 2,400, with 1,800 allowed only with touchdown zone and centerline lights, or with an autopilot, FD or HUD [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9i1(a)]]. The RVR 5000 note is only for S-LOC 27 Category D with the MALSR out.

questions.q: You are cleared for the ILS RWY 7L approach, side-step to Runway 7R. Which statement about the side-step is true?
options: You fly to an MDA, and you still meet stepdown fix altitudes
You use the 7L DA, since you fly the ILS glideslope
You use the circling minimums, since you change runways
You fly to an MDA, but stepdown altitudes no longer apply
questions.why: Side-step minima are flown to an MDA, whatever approach is authorized. You are still expected to meet the stepdown fix altitudes after you start the side-step. The minimums are nonprecision, so they are higher than the ILS minimums to 7L but normally lower than circling [[33:447|AIM 5-4-19]].

questions.q: You go missed at the MAWP of an RNAV (GPS) approach with a non-WAAS receiver. The missed is a climbing left turn direct to a holding waypoint. Climbing out, the CDI shows a straight extension of the final course, and the distance from the MAWP keeps growing. What is going on?
options: The receiver lost RAIM and is now only advisory
The missed approach was activated too early
The receiver is flying the first leg of the missed
You did not sequence the receiver past the MAWP
questions.why: A non-WAAS GPS needs pilot action to sequence past the MAWP to the missed approach. If you don't, it shows an extension of the final approach course and the distance from the MAWP increases until you sequence it [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]]. Sequence it now and turn as published.

questions.q: An RNAV (GPS) chart has LPV and LNAV lines. Inside the FAF there is a stepdown fix marked LNAV only, with a minimum altitude. Your WAAS receiver shows LPV and you are following the glidepath. What about the stepdown altitude?
options: You must level at it until you pass the fix
It applies only if the weather is below 1,000 ft
It becomes your DA if the glidepath flags
It does not apply; it is for MDA lines only
questions.why: Stepdown altitudes inside the final approach segment apply only when you fly to an MDA line. They do not apply on LPV or LNAV/VNAV lines flown to a DA, because obstacle clearance there comes from following the vertical guidance. Outside the final segment you must honor them on any approach [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].

questions.q: Approach control offers you the GLS RWY 4 approach, circle to land RWY 22, because of a strong wind from the southwest. What do you say?
options: Unable: circling from a GLS is prohibited, so ask for another approach
Accept, using the GLS DA as your circling altitude
Accept, but use Category D circling visibility
Accept, as long as the chart lists circling minimums
questions.why: Circling from a GLS, from an ILS without a localizer line of minima, or from an RNAV (GPS) approach without an LNAV line of minima is prohibited [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]]. Tell ATC you are unable and ask for an approach that allows circling.

questions.q: At a non-towered field at night you keyed the mike 7 times at the IAF to turn on the pilot-controlled lights. Twenty minutes later you are about to cross the FAF. What should you do?
options: Nothing; the lights stay on until you land
Key the mike 7 times within 5 seconds again
Key the mike 3 times for full brightness
Ask Flight Service to turn the lights on
questions.why: Pilot-controlled lights stay on for 15 minutes from the most recent activation. Even if they look on, key the mike just before entering the final segment, starting with 7 times within 5 seconds for the highest intensity [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]]. Three times is the lowest intensity.

questions.q: Flying an RNAV (GPS) approach to LNAV minimums, you are 1 NM from the FAWP. The receiver still shows the armed (terminal) mode and never changed to approach mode. No RAIM message is shown. What do you do?
options: Descend anyway; with no RAIM message the GPS is fine
Hold altitude and wait for approach mode at the MAWP
Don't descend; fly to the MAWP via the FAWP and go missed
Turn now toward the missed approach holding fix
questions.why: If the receiver does not sequence into approach mode before the FAWP, you must not start the approach or descend. Fly to the MAWP via the FAWP, fly the missed approach and tell ATC as soon as practical [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]]. Failing to sequence may mean a satellite problem [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(6)]].

questions.q: You plan the Daggett RNAV (GPS) RWY 26 shown. On the missed you expect 90 knots groundspeed, and today your airplane can climb only about 300 fpm. Which minimums should you plan to use?
options: LPV DA 2,438 ft with 1¾ mile visibility
LPV DA# 2,217 ft, since 300 fpm is close enough
LNAV MDA 2,700 ft, since both LPV lines need 220 ft/NM
None; the approach is not authorized for you
questions.why: 300 fpm at 1.5 NM a minute is only 200 ft per NM. The # line needs 220 ft per NM to 8,000, which is 330 fpm at 90 knots [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. When you can't make the steeper gradient, use the higher line that needs only the standard climb [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]: LPV DA 2,438 with 1¾ mile.

questions.q: Your airplane has no VREF and a VSO of 66 knots. In gusty wind you will circle at 100 knots. The circling line shows the white C in a black square, and the circling MDA is 980 ft MSL. What circling radius protects you?
options: 1.3 NM
1.5 NM
1.8 NM
1.7 NM
questions.why: 1.3 × 66 = 85.8 knots, so the airplane is Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. At 100 knots you are past the 91-knot top of Category A, so use Category B [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]. The C symbol means the expanded table: Category B with an MDA of 1,000 ft MSL or less is 1.7 NM [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]. 1.5 NM is the old standard Category B radius.

questions.q: Flying a straight-in LNAV approach with a VDP, you level at the MDA and see the runway clearly 1 NM before the VDP. What is the best plan?
options: Descend now, since the runway is in sight
Stay level until the MAP, then descend
Stay at the MDA until the VDP, then descend
Go missed, since you saw it before the VDP
questions.why: You should not descend below the MDA before the VDP, the point where a stable visual descent to touchdown can begin [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. Waiting until the MAP is a poor plan too: a descent between the VDP and the MAP may be unwise or impossible [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h3]].

questions.q: At 800 ft above the runway on an ILS, you are one dot above the glideslope and 8 knots slower than your target speed. Using energy management, which control fixes this best?
options: Throttle: add power to gain both height and speed
Elevator: lower the nose to trade height for speed
Throttle: reduce power to get down to the path
Elevator: raise the nose to slow the descent
questions.why: High and slow means the total energy is about right but split wrongly between altitude and airspeed. Distribution errors are fixed with the elevator, trading height for speed. Total energy errors (low and slow, high and fast) are fixed with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

questions.q: On vectors for a LOC RWY 36 approach, your only VHF nav receiver fails. Your IFR-approved GPS has a current database. What should you do?
options: Fly the LOC using the GPS moving map for course guidance
Fly the LOC approach as a GPS overlay from the database
Tell ATC about the failure and ask for an approach your GPS can fly
Continue the LOC approach and report the failure after landing
questions.why: LOC, LDA and SDF procedures are not authorized as GPS overlays [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17b5(a)]]. Report the malfunction to ATC as soon as practical, including the equipment affected and how it limits you [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. Then request an approach your equipment can fly, such as an RNAV (GPS).

questions.q: Circling to land at a non-towered airport, you are below the MDA past the MAP when a deer runs onto the runway. You go around but can't reach ATC on the radio down low. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Climb straight ahead on runway heading until ATC answers
Hold over the airport at the MDA until you can call ATC
Rejoin a published segment of the missed, its route and altitudes
Turn at once to the missed approach fix by the shortest way
questions.why: Going around from below the MDA or from a circle, the published missed may not give obstacle clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Get an amended clearance from ATC as soon as possible. If you can't, try to rejoin a published segment of the missed approach and follow its route and altitude instructions [[33:452|AIM 5-4-21h]]. At a non-towered field, fly the go-around without delay and contact ATC when able [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]].

questions.q: You break out of a 1,800 ft overcast with 4 miles visibility on a VOR approach that requires a circle to land. The circling MDA is 500 ft above the airport. What does the IFH suggest?
options: Circle at the MDA to stay as close to the runway as you can
Leave the MDA as soon as you see the airport
Climb back into the clouds to fly a wide downwind
Circle nearer pattern altitude, staying inside your radius
questions.why: Circling minimums are only minimums. If the ceiling allows, fly at an altitude closer to the VFR traffic pattern altitude: maneuvering is safer and the runway looks more normal [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. Stay inside the circling radius for your category [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f4]].

questions.q: After an earlier missed approach, you are cleared to land on your second ILS. Tower adds: caution wake turbulence, Boeing 757 departing the same runway. Where should you plan to touch down?
options: Well before the 757's rotation point
Beyond the 757's rotation point
On its touchdown point, at the aiming point
Anywhere, since departing wakes settle quickly
questions.why: Landing behind a larger airplane departing the same runway, note its rotation point and land well prior to it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b4]]. Its wake starts where it rotates. You are expected to adjust your path whether or not ATC warns you [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6a]].

questions.q: On vectors for an ILS you are high, and the glideslope centers while you are still outside the glideslope intercept point. A stepdown fix ahead, before the FAF, has an at-or-above altitude. You decide to track the glideslope down. What is true?
options: The glideslope guarantees every altitude before the FAF
You must still meet the stepdown fix's altitude
Stepdown altitudes don't apply once on the glideslope
You must not track the glideslope until the FAF
questions.why: The glideslope is meant to be intercepted at the glideslope intercept altitude, which marks the start of the final approach segment. Tracking it earlier does not ensure you meet the altitudes for preceding fixes, so you stay responsible for each stepdown altitude [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5b NOTE 2]].

questions.q: An RNAV (GPS) chart shows the note Visual Segment- Obstacles in the profile instead of a VDA. Your GPS still shows advisory vertical guidance. You are at the LNAV MDA with the runway in sight. What is true below the MDA?
options: The advisory guidance keeps you clear of obstacles
With no VDA, you may not descend below the MDA
You must use the guidance down to the runway
Following that path may lead you into obstacles
questions.why: That note replaces the VDA when obstacles below the MDA would force you off the angle. Pilots who follow the descent angle from the RNAV system below the MDA may meet obstacles, and must avoid them visually [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k1]]. There is no built-in obstacle protection from the MDA to touchdown [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

questions.q: A NOTAM puts a preplanned alternate missed approach into effect for the approach you will fly. The chart shows its holding pattern but no instructions. What is true?
options: It is optional; fly the published missed unless ATC says
It applies only if ATC reads it to you on frequency
It is mandatory, and the NOTAM gives its text and equipment
It replaces only the holding pattern, not the climb
questions.why: Alternate missed approach instructions are not printed on the chart, though the holding pattern may be shown. When a NOTAM puts it in effect, it becomes a mandatory part of the procedure, and the NOTAM gives the text and any extra equipment needed [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21e]].

questions.q: Weather is at the straight-in minimums for Runway 9, with a 10-knot tailwind. Circling to Runway 27 would put you into the wind. Your POH no-wind landing distance is 1,500 ft. About what distance do you need straight in on Runway 9?
options: About 1,650 ft
About 1,815 ft
About 1,500 ft
About 2,100 ft
questions.why: The first 10 knots of tailwind add about 21% to the landing distance [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. 1,500 × 1.21 = 1,815 ft. Weigh that against the circle into the wind before you start the approach.

questions.q: On a missed approach in light icing, your airplane climbs only 350 fpm at 90 knots groundspeed. The missed needs the standard 200 ft per NM. What is true?
options: You meet the gradient, but tell ATC you can't climb 500 fpm
You meet the gradient and need not tell ATC anything
You must level off and hold until the ice is gone
You can't meet the gradient, so declare an emergency
questions.why: At 90 knots you cover 1.5 NM a minute, so 200 ft per NM needs 300 fpm [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. 350 fpm meets that. But you should report to ATC, without being asked, when you are unable to climb at least 500 fpm [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(c)]].
